items.title: Long Wave
items.summary: R uth sets the children to dig for coins under the cushions of the ratty green sofa while she tries to get enough swimsuits and towels together. There is a big chest of drawers JP dragged home gleefully one evening, the scraping sound of her approaching, hollering for help. One of the other women, Sally, took it out into the concrete yard and sanded it down, repainted it, and then stenciled red flowers around the edges. As the women chopped carrots and argued about the rota, the children sneaked out at dusk and stuck their hands in the paint pot, left prints all over the front of the drawers. They get kids’ clothes from boxes on the street, charity sales and donations, and none of them fit right or they give way almost immediately at the seams but get shoved, nonetheless, into the chest of drawers and tugged out at random to put on whichever child needs them. Ori likes to go in by herself and dig thoughtfully through, chucking rejected dungarees and tie‑dye T‑shirts over her shoulder, plopping down on her backside to wrangle on leggings. Most of the swimsuits are nearly see-through from washing, the straps snapped, but Ruth manages to find enough and takes a handful of towels off the banister, puts them into the bag. The sun cream is out of date but will do the job. When she gets back into the sitting room, the cushions have been heaved off the sofa and everyone is bouncing on the wheezing springs. They have uncovered crushed breadsticks and molding apple cores but also a handful of lost 20-pence pieces, just enough for them all to get into the lido if she lies about some of their ages. She has been working all week, but today she is in charge. Ori rushes over and burbles something about jumping as high as the trees like a bird—no, like a dragon—and then tugs a pirate hat down as far as it will fit onto Ruth’s head. Let’s go, let’s go, she shouts, and everyone gathers, grabbing at shoes. There is Ori, who is 3—dressed this morning in a rainbow unicorn outfit with a wilting horn and a grubby tail—and Nora, with her shoes on the wrong feet, and Leo, who is 9 and an expert at making mayonnaise-and‑cheese sandwiches and wrapping them in foil. Last time they went to the lido he stole a rubber ring and he wears it slung around his middle now, hitching it up with one hand when it slithers down to his knees. There is also Bee, who is nearly 2 and who Ruth puts up on her hip to get out the door, and Tsembi, who is 7 and has a younger brother, Douglas, who bends to shit in his nappy beside the step, grunting intently. Sally has been making planters out of pallets to try to make some more money and they are stacked up outside the house with for sale signs pinned to them. Ruth and the kids make it down to the path and go in a ragtag, snaky line away from the house, Ruth yelling hold hands, hold hands, until everyone is pinned to someone else and trailing along. There isn’t enough cash for the bus. They’ll walk. Ruth hitches Bee onto her shoulders and Leo and Tsembi take turns carrying Douglas. The walk takes a long time. She changes Douglas’s nappy while the others climb onto the back of a bus-stop bench and compare war wounds. Douglas’s shit is runny and filled with little white worms again. It won’t be long before the others get them too. Ori is yelling loudly about being the fastest, fastest, fastest one and twisting back and forth to show off her scrapes and bumps, her multiple Moomin Band-Aids, which are grubby and starting to peel. Leo is hanging near her, his fingers beginning to tap a little in the way they do when everything is too loud and busy, his eyes glazing; Ruth calls him closer, tries to distract him, asks him to pass her cloths and then take the dirty nappy to a bin. Nora and Ori are arguing about who can stand on the back of the bench the longest without holding on. Bee is crouching and prodding at a snail nearby while Tsembi shouts at her to give it a rest, he’s only little, give it a rest. They make it to the pool. At the turnstile she counts heads and shoves the handful of coins in. They throw their towels down onto the brown grass and the kids strip their clothes off and fight over swimming costumes. She slathers sun cream on arms and legs and tries to stop Bee from falling in. Douglas examines his willy with his legs in the air and cries when a fat bee stings him on his round little belly. She scoops him up in one arm and gives him a sandwich. The older children are wading into the shallow end and lifting the water up in their hands and throwing it at one another, and Leo is dunking his head beneath the surface, where it must be good and quiet. Ori is leaping from the side over and over again, the force of her body leaving an after‑star‑shape in the air. Ruth gives Bee a sandwich too and puts on her own costume. It is one of JP’s and cuts in around the shoulders. Her mind is a rushing thing, trying to keep everyone in sight, tallying up who has sun cream on, thinking about what needs doing that day back at the house, thinking about the wood lice that have infested the room where she, JP, Leo, Nora and Ori sleep, which seem to dig their way up through the floors. There is a leak coming through the roof when it rains and sewage down the wall in the concrete yard whenever anyone upstairs flushes the chain. One night she woke, damp with sweat. JP was beside her on the blow‑up mattress and Leo and Nora were sprawled across the single beds, but when she looked again, Ori was not there. Ruth went out into the corridor. There was noise from the rooms above, which are rented out separately by students whom they almost never see, only hear. She had a sudden damp nightmare vision of Ori being spirited away or, rather, having never existed—she had never had a child. Sometimes, when she was pregnant, she had wished her away and now she was gone, she had never even been. She ran down the stairs. The front door was swinging wide and there was a white square of mucky moon and streetlight across the floor. Someone—one of the students—had left a half‑finished wine bottle on the front step. Ori was not in the yard among the stacked, unsold planters and experimental wooden birdhouses. A noise from the sitting room. Cheerios crunched under her feet. Ori was bent over in the corner, drawing with an imaginary pencil on the floor, talking quietly to herself. When Ruth pressed gently on her spine she sagged into Ruth’s arms, closed her eyes. That was the first time she walked in her sleep. The next day Ruth went and screamed at the hungover students, who came blearily out of their pizza-stinking rooms and scowled at her. Close the fucking front door, what is wrong with you? R uth tried everything to stop Ori from leaving the room at night. She tied her hands together by the wrists, she slept in front of the bedroom door, but always, somehow, Ori slipped free and Ruth would wake to her gone. It was a daytime and a nighttime problem. She was, JP said in exasperation after another desperate loudspeaker callout in the supermarket, a runner. Where had she gotten it from? This speedy, goat-like need to escape? Often, at the point of realizing she was lost, she would sit and wail. When they found her, she would be beside herself: You lost me, where were you? Ruth found herself thinking of the nights when the door of her childhood bedroom was locked against escape and she would knock on the walls and it would mean, I am here, I am here, are you there? One breakfast she undid the tie from JP’s dressing gown and rummaged around in the cupboard. The children were at the table, spoons hovering over their porridge, rumpled from sleep, watching her with suspicion. Ruth dug out a saucepan lid and tied it around Ori’s neck, gave her a metal spoon to bash it with. Ori’s eyes grew wide and she stood up on her chair. Bang , bang , bang , went the spoon on the saucepan, bang , bang , bang . That’s loud, JP said, holding closed her dressing gown. Well, we can hear where she is now,

items.summary: T hree thousand two hundred pages into Sarah J. Maas’s A Court of Thorns and Roses series, I became very worried that I was missing something. I had read close to the page-count equivalent of Proust’s In Search of Lost Time , but by the end of the latest entry, A Court of Splintered Harmony , published last month, my head was spinning. All of the human queens were a muddle for me. Had I missed the locations of the three kingdoms with which our heroes were locked in a diplomatic stalemate? And who, exactly, was Bryce? Half of all Americans don’t finish even a book a year, and yet millions of people in this country have read the six ACOTAR novels . Over the past few months, as I embarked on the task of joining those millions, I found the series everywhere. Readers wanted to talk about it with me while white-water tubing in West Virginia; a high-school classmate dissected the plot via Instagram DM; the books came up at a friend’s house party and on a bachelorette trip. These friends and acquaintances, along with so many others, have read—or will soon finish— Splintered Harmony (and then await, in January, its forthcoming 896-page sequel, A Court of Forgotten Melody ). Surely, they aren’t as baffled by its swirl of plots and characters as I am. I’d set out on my journey through Prythian, Maas’s faerie realm, in hopes of understanding what made both earnest fans of genre fiction and women I had never considered bookish tear through so many pages in so many numbers. I consider myself a close and deliberate reader, and I’m not a snob—I enjoy both fantasy and romance. But all of my attempts to decipher the Maas magic seemed to fail: I’d either work myself up about the incoherence of her society’s rules and history, or I’d bounce off the text altogether, like a kid sliding down the smooth sides of an inflatable castle. That feeling frustrated me—until I realized I’d been reading it wrong. There are, undeniably, ACOTAR obsessives—people who know all about the history of Prythian and its courts, and who instantly recognized Bryce Quinlan, a crossover character from another Maas series. Plenty of fans read, analyze, highlight, and speculate on social media. But it seems unlikely that they could make up the majority of the people who bought 1.7 million copies of Splintered Harmony on the day of its release. [ Read: Don’t call them trash ] After I’d finished submerging myself in reams of ACOTAR , a different possibility came to mind: The average fan isn’t overly concerned with all these details—and that’s fine, because these books don’t need you to be. They encourage a new kind of reading, more akin to the Marvel Cinematic Universe than the best-selling worlds of J. K. Rowling, James Patterson, or Jackie Collins . They travel differently too: A core of Easter-egg hunters spreads the word to casual fans, who are drawn mostly to the spectacle. Maas’s books aren’t the first blockbusters designed to be flipped through passively, maybe on a beach or with your phone in hand, but the bifurcated readership is noteworthy. You can choose to lock in, or you can sit back and offer up nothing but your presence and passive delight. The second path, I would argue, is more rewarding. W e might be at the end of reading, as my colleague Rose Horowitch reported pessimistically in July. The desire—and ability—to consume books for pleasure is dwindling, by many metrics, and scientists warn that phones are rotting our attention spans . In this environment, the success of ACOTAR , a doorstop series with no film or television adaptation, might seem puzzling. It follows a human girl, Feyre, who gets caught up in the drama of the faerie world next door; she initially falls in love with one hunky Fae man, only to leave him and marry the smoldering bad boy she’d told him not to worry about. By the time of Splintered Harmony , Feyre and her two sisters have all been turned into faeries and live in the magical realm. She’s the High Lady of the Night Court alongside her mate, Rhysand, and they have a six-month-old baby. There are ancient rites, magical weapons, and prophetic seers. And there is a fair amount of sex: Since 2015, when the first book was released, the series has become the poster child for the romantasy boom . A surface-level way to understand these books’ popularity is to assume that readers are there for the smut; having grown up with fantasy, they’re ready—and eager—for a mature version of it. That’s certainly a selling point, but compared with similar entries in the genre, Maas’s books are fairly tame, with a very high plot-to-horniness ratio. And many of the fans I’ve met will admit, cheerfully, that the sex isn’t all that earthshaking. (The sex scenes are also where Maas shows off some of her most awkward tics; she insists, for example, on calling a character’s orgasm their “release.”) Maas, I think, is offering readers something different—a genuinely epic story that goes down like a Netflix binge, one you can half pay attention to and still robustly enjoy. Like the MCU, it sets off enough fireworks to hook distracted readers who couldn’t care less who Bryce is, but unlike, say, Patterson, ACOTAR isn’t propelled by the question of what will happen next. Instead, Maas offers a kind of second-screen reading: rich in detail but low on crucial narration that cannot be missed. [ Read: The rise of must-read TV ] I don’t mean to imply that she’s making scenes skippable on purpose. Everything Maas has written suggests that she cares about building and expanding her magical realms, that she’s thought about the origins of Prythian’s kingdoms, and that she intends to resolve some of the series’ mysteries. Nor do I believe that she’s being asked by her editors to whittle down or simplify her lore to boost sales (in fact, the sprawling faerie world just keeps expanding, to the series’ detriment). It’s just that her building blocks aren’t all load-bearing, in part because they seem interchangeable. Men will “growl” their lines of dialogue many times in the series, and a reader’s eyes will barely register it—except at clearly signposted moments (as when Rhysand growls at Feyre, “Don’t bother buttoning up that nightgown”). Splintered Harmony frequently mentions Rask, Montesere, and Vallahan, three kingdoms our heroes hope to recruit to their war effort. But the main characters don’t go there; they just partake in a summit held on neutral ground. This fateful conference has the potential to generate tense, plot-heavy moments of court intrigue and diplomacy. Instead, in the Maas style, the reader can lean back and watch the prose float by. For a long chapter, Rhys, Feyre, and their friend Morrigan try to win over a variety of royal figures, all of whom are introduced (with their clothing) at length: “Well,” the golden-haired Queen of Vallahan said, her blue eyes as frozen as the icy mountains of her territory. Nestled in her heavy cloak of furs, a braided circlet of gold across her pale brow and tattooed runes running down her long, bony fingers, she cut an imposing figure. Though no weapons adorned her, there was something about her direct gaze, her stillness, that radiated warrior . Perhaps not one who’d fight on battlefields, but one who would kill to defend what was hers. That gaze now fixed wholly on me. A few pages later, negotiations have not quite begun. We get a sumptuous description of the fruits our trio have brought to the summit. We linger on more outfits. Things start to heat up; a few barbs are traded. But then a new character is introduced; another outfit needs describing. Okay, time to start negotiating—except now Feyre has a flashback to a character introduced in the first book, and then she’s thinking back to the arc that made up most of the second and third books. For the rest of the chapter, gorgeous gowns, creeping magical tendrils, and billowing shadows wash over the reader. items.title: How to navigate the world with two halves of one brain
items.summary: Psychiatrist Iain McGilchrist has spent 35 years studying how the brain shapes consciousness. In this full interview, he explains why the two hemispheres attend to the world in radically different ways, and how one narrow, grasping mode has come to dominate Western civilization. He then explores the nature of reality: a creative cosmos that flows at the edge of chaos, where consciousness is primary and matter is one of its phases. He closes with what makes a human life flourish. This video How to navigate the world with two halves of one brain is featured on Big Think .

items.summary: Rumor has it that now—in our world of alternative facts, of journalists replaced by influencers, experts replaced by AI, and of news constantly deemed fake—we’ve finally, finally done away with that dastardly thing called “truth.” Hard data is tough to come by, since sensationalism’s better for algorithms. It’s difficult to tell if any given video is secretly an ad. Not even our Google searches can be trusted. They’re calling it a “post-truth society,” and here we are, left in constant skepticism over the fabric of our reality. Did we really have a White House Press Secretary between October 12th and October 16th, 2026? Is Manon of KATSEYE really on “hiatus”? Could we really “see everything”? Ugh. We can’t even trust our documentaries anymore. Multi-award-winning, National Book Award longlisted author Nafissa Thompson-Spires knows none of this is new. Her second book and debut novel, The Four Wives and Five Deaths of Richard Milford (a current First Novel Prize finalist) is set in the all-Black town of 1920s Newville, where the town has finally, finally done away with that dastardly thing called “Richard Milford.” An infamous moonshiner, an unloyal womanizer, and just plain mean, the town will tell you—collectively—that this is good riddance. That is, except for his four wives and his beloved housekeeper Alberta. They’d surely remember him differently, right? Unless they somehow had reason to kill him . . . Wait, how many times did Rich die? With slick wit, a wry sense of dark humor, and a hefty dose of whimsy, Thompson-Spires deconstructs the idea of truth before our very eyes in this tightly wrapped satire/whodunnit. Over Zoom, the author and I discussed how our imaginations can deceive us, the careful game of Black satire, John Edgar Wideman’s concept of “Great Time,” and how she brought herself back to play after years of fearing the sophomore slump. Jalen Giovanni Jones : Your previous book, the short story collection Heads of the Colored People , grappled with being Black in a world that constantly gaslights you. Given that The Four Wives and Five Deaths of Richard Milford interrogates our notion of a concrete truth, I’m curious to know if you were expanding on those ideas that you set up in your first book. Nafissa Thompson-Spires: You know, I was. All these women in the book have been gaslit in many different ways. The town of Newville is gaslighting, too, when it comes to how they approach Rich—how they think about his trauma, and how they see him as this cursed, evil figure that they’re happy to be rid of. And gaslighting plays a huge part in how the book’s climax manifests. My writing is still interested in that overall project. JGJ : What was your experience like, transitioning from short story writing to novel writing? Do you find your approach to be vastly different between each form? Once I have the structure, then I know what I’m doing. NTS: They were very different at first. I found novel writing really difficult. God bless all the people who can write novels, who can just pop them out so quickly. This book took me five years. It’s a slim book, but ultimately my editors gave me some good advice—to lean into my talents as a short story writer, and to lean into what made Heads work, in order to write this book. That’s why the book consists of short chapters that are almost standalone, yet are all linked in their own way. The process for me involved a lot of prayer, a lot of worrying, a lot of fretting. Things really crystallized, though, when I told RO Kwon that I really wanted to make Richard Milford die in five different ways. I was really stuck on the structure, but she was like “well why don’t you make him die five different ways?” After those deaths dictated the structure, everything else came together. That’s true for my stories in general—once I have the structure, then I know what I’m doing. JGJ : Speaking of structure, you take on many different POVs throughout the novel—six perspectives, which is impressive in under 200 pages. How’d you know which perspectives to include, and when? NTS: I knew I wanted all of the women to have a part, including the housekeeper Alberta. I organized it by each death—who held the first baton in the murder-relay race, and then who passed it off to the next person, and to the next. Alberta specifically is central to the book because she’s known Rich all his life. She can speak to how he was as a child in the same way that the town of Newville can, but with more intimacy and perhaps more honesty, because I think Newville gets a lot of things wrong. Newville brought a tall tale quality to the novel’s structure, which built out as I thought more about who I wanted Rich to be. Initially he started as an attempt to satirize the traditional trauma plot. But I wanted to write his traumas without limiting his backstory to solely those experiences. He has so many different things that you can blame for his bad behavior, all of them outlandish: getting thrown from a horse, getting struck by lightning, the murder-suicide of his parents, being double dipped during his baptism, and so on. I wanted to play with origin stories, to question how we become who we are. JGJ: I took note of the novel’s tall-tale quality. Even though I’d call it realist, it still has elements of the fantastical and surreal. There’s lightning strikes, visions that people are having, and Rich just refuses to actually die. Were you intentionally turning away from realism with this novel? NTS: I’m not sure it was an intentional turn away from realism, but I knew that I wanted the realism to be spiced and peppered with that magic. I was really thinking of tall tales and fables, and how somebody can grow so big in your mind that they’re no longer a real person to you. I was hesitant to do that with Rich at first, because I didn’t want to feed into the idea of an “invincible Black man who can’t be killed, can’t be tamed.” I wanted to write a Black man who was a real person, as much as he was a figment of people’s imaginations. That’s part of what the book is satirizing—how we think about Black men as indestructible. Why do police have to shoot Black men at all? Why so many times? Why taze and shoot and kick? All of those mini-deaths that Rich dies are part of that commentary. The way that he won’t die is part of this questioning of why the Black man lives this way in the figments of our imagination. JGJ: The idea of a person can end up becoming something entirely separate from who they are in reality. I see that manifesting a lot in today’s world especially. So what was it that made you want to set this novel in the 1920s? That’s part of what the book is satirizing—how we think about Black men as indestructible. NTS: I wanted an all-Black town. I knew that from the very beginning. This story is based on my real life great-grandfather, who grew up in the 30s and 40s, had 40 children and three wives, and beat them all with a horse whip. I wanted to see what it would be like for the women in his life to get revenge on him. My great grandfather was known as both a menace in his town, as well as this beloved figure. I wanted to hold space for both of those things, and setting the story in an all-Black town had the locale that could. Oklahoma made the most sense because it historically had 50 all-Black towns, and only 13 of them remain. That’s where Newville’s goal for self-preservation came into play—the idea that people are competing for versions of the truth, because they’re competing to be historicized, to make sure that they’re remembered and have a legacy. I wanted to draw attention to the legacies of these real-life towns as well, because so many of them—while remembered by the people who live near them—are forgotten by history in so many ways. items.title: 8 size and distance comparisons: from subatomic to cosmic
items.summary: Here in this Universe, there are multiple different ways to look at all that exists in terms of size. You can look at the physical size, or volumes, that the objects occupy, and you can do that in a variety of ways. For humans, we can measure our dimensions — things like our height, width, and depth — or the amount of volume we displace when placed in a bath of water. Whichever method we choose, we get a proxy for our size. For planets, we can look at the edges of their solid surfaces or atmospheres; for stars, we can look at the boundary of their photospheres; for atoms, we probe them through techniques like force microscopy or scattering experiments. But in addition to these physical sizes, we can also examine such objects relative to other objects of the same type as found in nature. We can look at the distance from one human to another, for example, under a variety of common conditions. We can examine the distances between atoms, or stars, or planets, or galaxies, or anything else that we choose. And if we like, one interesting comparison that we can make, on any scale we choose, is the ratio between the physical size of the object itself to the distance from it to the next similar object. If we were to do this, which scale would be the most extreme, and how does that relate to human scales that we’re familiar with? Let’s examine eight different scales, from the quantum to the cosmic, to find out. Although, by volume, an atom is mostly empty space, dominated by the electron cloud, the dense atomic nucleus, responsible for only 1 part in 10^15 of an atom’s volume, contains ~99.95% of an atom’s mass. Reactions between internal components of a nucleus can be more precise and occur on shorter timescales, as well as at different energies, than transitions restricted to an atom’s electrons. Credit : Yzmo and Mpfiz/Wikimedia Commons 1.) Subatomic scales On scales smaller than an atom, we run into things like atomic nuclei, electrons, individual protons or neutrons within the nucleus, and quarks and gluons. Of these particles, it’s not necessarily fair to talk about “size” for most of them: quarks, gluons, and electrons are consistent with being what we call point particles, or particles consistent with having an actual size of 0. From scattering experiments, we’ve determined that if they do have a size, that size is no larger than about 10 -19 meters, or a tenth of an attometer. Protons, neutrons, and atomic nuclei, however, do have an actual size: about that of a femtometer, or 10 -15 meters. Within this context, you might consider looking at the distance from one subatomic particle — like a proton or the nucleus — to an electron as a measure of distance on subatomic scales. (If you went to look between two protons in the same nucleus, you’d find that they were practically adjacent: a distance-to-size ratio of around 1-to-1.) Since electrons are typically around a tenth of a nanometer, or 10 -10 meters, away from the nucleus, that results in a ratio of around 100,000-to-1. If the atomic nucleus were the size of a basketball located at Pepperdine University in Malibu, the electron would be roughly 24 kilometers (15 miles) away on the Santa Monica Pier. The K-4 crystal consists exclusively of carbon atoms arranged in a lattice, but with an unconventional bond angle compared to either graphite, diamond, or graphene. These inter-atomic properties can lead to drastically different physical, chemical, and material properties even with identical chemical formulas for a variety of structures. The average separation between two atoms in a lattice-like structure is only marginally larger than the size of one atom itself. Credit : Workbit/Wikimedia Commons 2.) Atomic scales Atoms are the building block of nearly everything we find on Earth, with enormous numbers of these very, very small entities combining together to compose the entire world and so much more. Atoms make up the atmosphere, the seas, the rocks and soil, every living creature on our planet, and the entire world itself, as well as pretty much every other known world in the Universe and much more. Atoms are generally the same physical size everywhere in the Universe — with the smallest atom, helium, having a diameter of 0.06 nanometers and the largest well-measured one, cesium, having a diameter of between 0.520 and 0.596 nanometers — with a typical atom’s size being around 10 -10 meters. But atoms can come in a huge variety of configurations, with some configurations placing atoms almost perfectly adjacent to one another and others creating great separations between them. Some examples include: in a water molecule, hydrogen and oxygen atoms are separated by 0.1 nanometers, in a diamond, two carbon atoms are separated by 0.15 nanometers, in the Earth’s crust, silicon and oxygen atoms are separated by 0.16 nanometers, and in a helium balloon, gaseous, monatomic helium atoms are typically separated by 3.4 nanometers. In solids and liquids, or wherever atoms are bound together into molecules, the next atom over is approximately only one or two atomic diameters away, while in a gas composed of atoms, the next atomic particle (at Earth’s standard pressure and temperature) is only a few dozen atom diameters away. If an atom again were a basketball on a basketball court, the next atom over for solids and liquids would be at the distance of a very tight defender, while for gases, the next atom over would be standing over by the 3-point line. Whereas ice requires water molecules to take on a relatively inefficient bond angle structure, even warm water achieves greater densities than ice does. At lower temperatures and higher pressures, liquid water is the densest form of water of all. The separation between water molecules in ocean water is approximately the same scale as the diameter of a water molecule itself. Credit : World Ocean Review 3.) Molecular scales This is an interesting one, because the separation distance between molecules depends tremendously on which type of molecules we’re talking about and the environment that they’re found in. Sure, when we think of molecules we typically think of something like water, which is a small molecule just 0.28 nanometers across: barely larger than an atom. But human DNA is also a molecule, albeit one that’s about three billion base pairs in length, spanning over a micron in length when coiled up (over 1000 nanometers) or extending for more than two meters if stretched out end-to-end. The protein Titin , found in striated muscle, is similarly large when coiled. But what about the distances between molecules? Again, the distance depends on the environment, and it varies tremendously. In red blood cells, the distance between hemoglobin molecules is about 7 nanometers, compared with the size of hemoglobin at about 5 nanometers. In the ocean, water molecules are separated by about 0.31 nanometers, compared to a size of 0.28 nanometers. Nitrogen molecules in Earth’s atmosphere at sea level are separated by 3.4 nanometers, while a nitrogen molecule is just 0.3 nanometers in size. In Mars’s carbon dioxide-rich but thin atmosphere, however, the average separation distance is more like 17 nanometers, compared to a molecular size of 0.3 nanometers. Although gases can be very sparse indeed, for most applications, if a molecule was the size of a basketball, the next molecule over would still be on the same basketball court, and in many cases, just around one basketball-diameter away. This crowd in Mauerpark, Berlin, is an excellent example of large numbers of people gathered together in one place: where the average separation distances between humans is small even compared to the scale of a single human.
